FOR YOU

Here is what your care team has decided about cognitive training and your quality of life.

Computer-based brain training is not a reason, on its own, to decide how your quality of life will change. Right now, the research does not show clearly whether it makes quality of life better, worse, or the same when people do it for at least 12 weeks compared with people who do not do it.

What this means for you:

- The research does not yet show a clear effect on quality of life, either way.
- If you would like to try cognitive training, we will mainly think of it as a way to work on specific thinking goals. We will choose those goals together with you.
- We will measure your quality of life when we start and again at follow-up, using the same questionnaire each time. This lets us see whether anything changes for you.
- We will review this plan when new evidence becomes available.

Claim: There is not enough evidence yet to say whether computer-based cognitive training of at least 12 weeks makes quality of life higher, lower, or the same compared with no training.

We do not yet know whether using the device with a therapist over video (telerehabilitation) or training on your own leads to people stopping use of the device at 3 months. The one study we have found that compares these approaches is small and was not designed to show small differences, so the answer is uncertain.

Claim: The evidence suggests no difference in device abandonment at 3 months between telerehabilitation with a therapist and self-guided training, but the certainty of this evidence is very low, so the result is uncertain.

What this means for you:
- Neither option is clearly better for stopping use of the device, so the choice is open.
- The best choice depends on what you prefer, whether you can get telerehabilitation, and how well you can use the device on your own.
- If you choose telerehabilitation, you will have regular contact with a therapist, and your use will be checked at 3 months.
- If you choose self-guided training, you will have a check at 3 months to see if you are still using the device and to offer help if you are not.
- The study was on a head-mounted low vision aid. Its results may not apply to you or to other devices.

Please talk with your clinician about which option suits you.

Right now, the research does not show whether negative pressure wound therapy (a dressing that uses gentle suction, set at 75 mmHg) raises, lowers, or leaves the chance of infection unchanged compared with standard care. The evidence on this is very uncertain, and the only study named is about serious dog bites to the arms or legs. It may not apply to your wound.

So your team will choose the dressing based on your local hospital guidelines and your own health factors. If standard care is used, you will get the usual wound care and infection checks for your type of wound. If the suction dressing is considered, your team will weigh it against other factors for your wound, and the record will note that any effect on infection is not yet proven.

Your wound will be checked at the follow-up times set by the local guidelines. Tell your care team right away if you notice spreading redness, warmth, swelling, pus, or fever. The decision can be revisited if better evidence becomes available.
